summary: Deep technical discussion about deploying Redwood Private into StratusHealth VPCs. Major topics: PrivateLink vs Transit Gateway, NAT/egress design, DNS resolution, subnet placement for inference nodes, KV cache and batching network implications, and quantization/latency tradeoffs. Agreed next steps: share checklist, PoC plan, and customer topology for a pilot.

transcript: 00:00 Sofia Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we, um, are going to dig into Private VPC networking and the runtime implications. Miguel is on to walk through design. 00:28 Miguel Santos: Hi all, quick agenda: private link options, nat/egress, dns, subnets, and then how KV cache and batching affect latency with cross-subnet traffic. 01:12 Rajiv Menon: Sounds good — we're mainly concerned about egress cost and compliance, we need no data plane traffic leaving our account for PII. 01:40 Miguel Santos: Right, for Private we have two primary network patterns: (1) PrivateLink endpoints to Redwood control plane + data plane proxied with ENIs or (2) Transit Gateway/VPN with customer-hosted routing. PrivateLink avoids NAT egress since traffic stays within AWS backbone. 02:12 Emily Carter: Quick clarif — when you say PrivateLink for the data plane, do you mean model inference tokens go via a VPC endpoint to Redwood-managed ENIs? 02:23 Miguel Santos: Yes, although implementation differs by deployment. For Strict on-prem/VPC we can run the inference runtime inside your VPC and only call back to control plane over PrivateLink; alternatively, a managed ENI model where traffic is peered. 02:50 Jordan Lee: Security concern — what about S3 access for models or model artifacts? We want kms-encrypted artifacts and no internet egress. 03:10 Anya Li: For artifacts, we recommend customer-managed model storage or an S3 VPC endpoint plus IAM role. The runtime can mount models from your S3 via VPC endpoint so no internet egress. 03:45 Rajiv Menon: Good. How does DNS work with PrivateLink? We have split-horizon DNS and internal zones. 04:05 Miguel Santos: We use conditional forwarding for the private endpoints. If you use AWS Private DNS with an interface endpoint, your VPC resolver will resolve the redwood endpoints internally. There are some gotchas with multiple zones and resolver rules. 04:32 Emily Carter: Yep, we use Route 53 Resolver endpoints for hybrid, and we need to know if Redwood will require changes to our resolver rules. 04:47 Sofia Patel: We'll provide a step-by-step network checklist — sample resolver rules, endpoint names, and expected ports. 05:05 Miguel Santos: Ports: primarily 443 for control plane and mutual TLS. For data plane streaming (gRPC), also 443 but we support ALPN negotiation; no unusual ports. 05:34 Priya Nair: About egress — we have a NAT gateway per private subnet and it gets expensive. Is there a way to avoid NAT for model traffic? 05:50 Miguel Santos: Yes, with PrivateLink and interface endpoints you avoid NAT for calls to Redwood. For external repos or OS package updates you'd still need NAT unless you provide a proxy. 06:15 Jordan Lee: And what about VPC peering vs Transit Gateway — which is better for multi-account setups? 06:28 Miguel Santos: Transit Gateway scales better for many accounts. PrivateLink is better for strict isolation and avoids routing table explosion; if you have many VPCs, TGW centralizes routing but careful with route propagation. 06:50 Rajiv Menon: For latency-sensitive workloads we worry about cross-AZ hops. where should inference nodes live? 07:05 Anya Li: Keep inference nodes in the same AZs as your application frontends if low-latency is critical. Also pin KV caches to the same AZ to avoid inter-AZ network penalties. 07:32 Miguel Santos: Right — KV cache affinity matters: cache misses require fetching from model shard or remote KV which adds tens of ms. If your prefixes are sticky and we can route to the same node/AZ, latency improves a lot. 08:00 Emily Carter: How does batching change this? Larger batches increase throughput but add tail latency, right? 08:14 Miguel Santos: Exactly. Batching improves tokens/sec but you add queueing latency. For 99th p99 targets we recommend small max batch size and dynamic batch thresholds. 08:36 Rajiv Menon: Any quantization impact we should be aware of in terms of network? 08:45 Miguel Santos: Quantization reduces memory and can change model sharding. Smaller model footprint can let you colocate more replicas in a single host, reducing cross-host traffic for KV and kv-cache. 09:05 Jordan Lee: For audit and logging — will traffic through PrivateLink still produce audit logs we can ingest? 09:18 Anya Li: Yes, we emit access logs and you can ship them to your logging endpoint over the PrivateLink. We also support S3 log delivery via VPC endpoints. 09:40 Emily Carter: What's the recommended subnet sizing and IP requirements per inference node? 09:50 Miguel Santos: Each containerized inference worker typically uses a few ENIs / IPs depending on host networking. For an autoscaling pool we recommend planning for peak concurrent requests and leave a ~20% cushion. We'll provide an IP planning worksheet. 10:15 Sofia Patel: We'll attach the worksheet and a sample CloudFormation/Terraform snippet for interface endpoints. 10:33 Rajiv Menon: Any concerns about throughput limits on interface endpoints? 10:40 Miguel Santos: Interface endpoints scale with ENIs and you hit per-ENI bandwidth. For very high throughput we recommend using multiple endpoints or a Transit Gateway pattern with internal load balancing. We'll propose option A/B in the PoC. 11:05 Priya Nair: For the PoC we'd like to run a baseline: 500 qps 256-token average workload, measure p50/p95/p99 and cost. 11:20 Miguel Santos: Good. That helps us configure batch sizes and concurrency. We'll propose test harness and synthetic load script. 11:40 Emily Carter: On the control plane side, what's the handshake? Is there mutual TLS and client certs? 11:50 Anya Li: Yes mutual TLS, and we support customer mTLS + SAML SCIM for auth. Credentials never leave your KMS if you use our Private deployment option integrated with your HSM. 12:12 Rajiv Menon: We need SOC2 and an architecture security brief for our auditors. 12:20 Sofia Patel: We'll send the security pack and SOC2 report, and redacted runbooks. 12:35 Jordan Lee: One more — what's the failover story if an AZ goes down? 12:44 Miguel Santos: We recommend cross-AZ replicas and a routing policy that can redirect traffic; caching and sticky routing needs fallback to remote node with higher latency but maintained correctness. 13:05 Priya Nair: About DNS again — will the runtime do SRV lookups or is it basic A records? We depend on SRV for some services. 13:18 Miguel Santos: We primarily rely on A/AAAA records with ALPN for service negotiation; we can support SRV for special cases but it's not the default. 13:40 Emily Carter: For the pilot, we'll want a checklist: endpoints to create, resolver rules, IAM roles, and expected ports. 13:52 Sofia Patel: Noted — we'll deliver that. 14:05 Miguel Santos: I'll also include latency tuning guidance: batch size, kv cache TTLs, and how to pin shards to AZs. 14:22 Rajiv Menon: Ok, can we also get an estimate of egress savings if we avoid NAT via PrivateLink? rough numbers are fine. 14:35 Miguel Santos: Yes we'll model that in the proposal; typical savings depend on your NAT/GW costs and data egress patterns, but PrivateLink usually reduces both latency and egress charges for large traffic volumes. 14:55 Emily Carter: Great. Anything else? 15:05 Sofia Patel: Quick recap — action items and we'll schedule the network deep-dive with your infra team next week. 15:22 Rajiv Menon: Thanks everyone. 15:28 Miguel Santos: Thanks, bye.
